html:
The emigration of people from Mount Lebanon and the Levant coast to the Americas, West Africa and beyond, which began in earnest in the 1880s and has never stopped. Today more people of Lebanese origin live abroad than in Lebanon itself.

The first big wave left the Ottoman province in the late 1800s. Many were Christian villagers, pushed by poverty, a crisis in the silk trade and memories of the communal fighting of 1860, and pulled by stories of fortunes made overseas. They often started as peddlers and then opened shops. Large communities grew in Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, the United States and Senegal and other parts of West Africa. The great famine of World War I drove more out.

Later waves followed the civil war of 1975 to 1990 and the wars and economic collapse since. The diaspora sends home money that keeps many families going.

Emigrants and their children have done well in their new homes. They include the writer Kahlil Gibran in the United States and the businessman Carlos Slim in Mexico.
sum: The emigration of people from Mount Lebanon and the Levant coast to the Americas, West Africa and beyond, which began in earnest in the 1880s and has never stopped. Today more people of Lebanese origin live abroad than in Lebanon itself.
